title: Part 1, Chapter 46
paragraphs: About the end of the notable adventure of the officers of the Holy Brotherhood; and the great ferocity of our worthy knight, Don Quixote

While Don Quixote was carrying on like this, the curate was trying to convince the officers that he was out of his mind, as they could see from his actions and his words, and that they need not press the matter — even if they arrested him and took him away, they'd have to release him before long as a madman. The officer holding the warrant replied that it was not his business to investigate Don Quixote's madness, only to carry out his superior's orders, and that once he had him in custody they could let him go three hundred times if they pleased.
"All the same," said the curate, "you mustn't take him away this time, and in my opinion he won't let himself be taken either."

In the end the curate argued so well, and Don Quixote did such mad things, that the officers would have been madder than he was if they hadn't recognised his lack of wits; so they thought it best to be pacified, and even to act as peacemakers between the barber and Sancho Panza, who were still bitterly arguing. In the end the officers, in their capacity as officers of justice, settled the matter by arbitration in such a way that both sides were, if not perfectly contented, at least somewhat satisfied: they swapped the pack-saddles but not the girths or head-stalls. As for Mambrino's helmet, the curate, on the quiet and without Don Quixote knowing, paid eight reals for the basin, and the barber wrote out a full receipt and an undertaking to make no further demand then or thereafter, forever, amen. With these two disputes — the most important — settled, all that remained was for Don Luis's servants to agree that three of them would go back while one stayed to accompany him wherever Don Fernando wanted to take him. Good luck and better fortune, having already begun to clear away difficulties and remove obstacles in favour of the lovers and warriors at the inn, were pleased to keep going and bring everything to a happy resolution: the servants agreed to do as Don Luis wished, which gave Doña Clara such happiness that no one could have looked into her face at that moment without seeing the joy in her heart. Zoraida, though she didn't fully understand all she was seeing, was grave or cheerful without knowing why, as she watched and studied the various faces — especially her Spaniard's, whom she followed with her eyes and clung to with her soul. The gift and compensation the curate had given the barber hadn't escaped the landlord's notice, and he demanded payment of Don Quixote's reckoning, plus the cost of the damage to his wine-skins and the loss of his wine, swearing that neither Rocinante nor Sancho's ass would leave the inn until he'd been paid down to the last farthing. The curate settled it all amicably, and Don Fernando paid — though the Judge had also been very ready to settle the bill. Everything became so peaceful and quiet that the inn no longer brought to mind the discord of Agramante's camp, as Don Quixote had put it, but the peace and tranquillity of the days of Octavianus. The universal opinion was that thanks were due to the great zeal and eloquence of the curate, and to the unexampled generosity of Don Fernando.

Now that he was clear of all quarrels — his squire's as well as his own — Don Quixote considered it would be wise to resume the journey he'd begun and bring to a close that great adventure for which he had been called and chosen. With this lofty resolve he went and knelt before Dorothea, who refused to let him say a word until he had risen; so to obey her he stood up and said, "There's a common proverb, fair lady, that 'diligence is the mother of good fortune,' and experience has often shown in important matters that the persistence of the negotiator brings a doubtful case to a successful end. But nowhere does this truth show itself more plainly than in war, where speed and decisiveness anticipate the enemy's schemes and win the victory before the foe has time to defend himself. I say all this, exalted and esteemed lady, because it seems to me that for us to remain any longer in this castle is useless now, and may yet prove harmful in some way we'll find out one day. Who's to say your enemy the giant has not learned by means of secret and diligent spies that I am going to destroy him? And if the chance is given him, he may take it to fortify himself in some impregnable castle or stronghold against which all my efforts and the might of my tireless arm might avail very little. So, lady, let us, as I say, forestall his schemes by our quickness, and depart at once in quest of fair fortune. Your highness is only being kept from enjoying it as fully as you'd wish by my delay in confronting your adversary."

Don Quixote fell silent and waited calmly for the beautiful princess's reply. With commanding dignity and in a style adapted to Don Quixote's own, she answered, "I thank you, sir knight, for the eagerness you show — like the good knight you are, to whom it's a natural obligation to help the orphan and the needy — to come to my aid in my sore trouble. And heaven grant that your wishes and mine may be fulfilled, so you may see there are women in this world capable of gratitude. As for my departure, let it be at once, for I have no will but yours. Dispose of me entirely as you see fit. She who has once entrusted to you the defence of her person, and placed in your hands the recovery of her kingdom, must not think of offering opposition to whatever your wisdom may decree."

"On then, in God's name," said Don Quixote, "for when a lady humbles herself to me, I will not miss the chance to raise her up and set her on the throne of her ancestors. Let us depart at once. The common saying that 'in delay there is danger' lends spurs to my eagerness to take the road. Since neither heaven has created nor hell has seen anything that can daunt or intimidate me, saddle Rocinante, Sancho, and get ready your ass and the queen's palfrey, and let us take leave of the castellan and these gentlemen and go this very instant."
Sancho, who had been standing by the whole time, said, shaking his head, "Oh, master, master, there's more mischief afoot in the village than gets talked about — saving the pardon of all good folk."
"What mischief can there be in any village, or in all the cities of the world, you booby, that can damage my reputation?" said Don Quixote.
"If your worship's getting angry," Sancho replied, "I'll hold my tongue and leave unsaid what a good squire is bound to say, and what a good servant should tell his master."

"Say what you like," Don Quixote returned, "so long as your words aren't meant to work on my fears. If you're afraid, you're behaving like yourself; but I'm behaving like myself, in not being afraid."

"It's nothing of the sort, as I'm a sinner before God," said Sancho, "but I take it as sure and certain that this lady, who calls herself queen of the great kingdom of Micomicón, is no more queen than my mother. If she were what she says, she wouldn't go rubbing noses every minute with a certain someone here behind every door."

Dorothea turned red at Sancho's words, because the truth was her husband Don Fernando had now and then, when others weren't looking, gathered from her lips some of the reward his love had earned, and Sancho, seeing this, had concluded that such liberties were more suited to a courtesan than to the queen of a great kingdom. Unable, or unwilling, to answer him, she let him go on, and he continued, "I say this, señor, because if after we've travelled roads and highways, gone through bad nights and worse days, one who's now enjoying himself in this inn is to reap the fruit of our labour, there's no rush for me to saddle Rocinante, put the pad on the ass, or get the palfrey ready. Better for us to stay put, and let every jade mind her spinning, and let's go to dinner."

Good God, what was Don Quixote's outrage when he heard his squire's brazen words! So great that, in a voice strangled with rage, his tongue stammering and his eyes flashing live fire, he exclaimed, "Rascally clown, boorish, insolent, ignorant, foul-mouthed, impudent backbiter and slanderer! How dare you utter such words in my presence and that of these noble ladies? How dare you harbour such gross and shameless thoughts in your muddled imagination? Get out of my sight, you born monster, storehouse of lies, hoard of untruths, granary of dirty tricks, inventor of scandals, broadcaster of absurdities, enemy of the respect due to royal persons! Get out, and don't appear before me again on pain of my fury." Saying this, he knitted his brows, puffed out his cheeks, glared around him, and stamped his right foot violently on the ground, displaying in every way the rage pent up in his heart. At his words and furious gestures Sancho was so terrified that he would have been glad if the earth had opened on the spot and swallowed him, and his only thought was to turn and bolt from the angry presence of his master.

But the quick-witted Dorothea, by now thoroughly familiar with Don Quixote's habit of mind, said, to soothe his wrath, "Don't be irritated, Knight of the Rueful Countenance, at the absurdities your good squire has uttered. Perhaps he didn't speak without cause; given his good sense and Christian conscience, it's unlikely he'd bear false witness against anyone. We may therefore believe, without hesitation, that since — as you yourself say, sir knight — everything in this castle goes on by means of enchantment, Sancho may well have seen, through this diabolical medium, what he claims to have seen, so much to the detriment of my modesty."

"I swear by God Almighty," exclaimed Don Quixote, "your highness has hit the mark; some vile illusion must have appeared before this sinner of a Sancho that made him see what couldn't otherwise be seen except by enchantment. I know perfectly well, from the poor fellow's goodness and harmlessness, that he is incapable of bearing false witness against anybody."

"True, no doubt," said Don Fernando, "and for that reason, Señor Don Quixote, you ought to forgive him and restore him to the bosom of your favour, _sicut erat in principio_, before illusions of this kind had taken away his senses."

Don Quixote said he was ready to pardon him, and the curate went to fetch Sancho, who came in very meekly, fell on his knees, and begged for his master's hand. Don Quixote gave it to him, allowed him to kiss it, then gave him his blessing and said, "Now, Sancho my son, you'll be convinced of the truth of what I have told you so often — that everything in this castle is done by enchantment."
"So I believe," said Sancho, "except the business of the blanket, which really happened by ordinary means."

"Don't believe it," said Don Quixote, "for if it had been so, I would have avenged you that instant, or even now; but neither then nor now could I, and I have not seen anyone on whom to avenge your wrong."

They were all curious to know what the blanket business was, and the landlord gave them a detailed account of Sancho's flights through the air, at which they laughed a great deal. Sancho would have been just as embarrassed if his master hadn't once more assured him it was all enchantment. For all that, his simple-mindedness never reached such a pitch that he could convince himself it wasn't the plain and simple truth, without any deception about it, that he'd been blanketed by beings of flesh and blood and not by visionary, imaginary phantoms, as his master believed and insisted.

The illustrious company had now been two days at the inn, and as it seemed time to leave, they devised a plan so that, without putting Dorothea and Don Fernando to the trouble of going back with Don Quixote to his village under pretext of restoring Queen Micomicona, the curate and the barber might carry him off with them as they had proposed, and the curate could try to take his madness in hand at home. To put the plan into action, they arranged with the owner of an ox-cart who happened to be passing to carry Don Quixote as follows. They built a kind of cage of wooden bars, big enough to hold him comfortably. Then Don Fernando and his companions, Don Luis's servants, and the officers of the Brotherhood, together with the landlord, all under the curate's directions, covered their faces and disguised themselves in various ways so as to appear to Don Quixote completely different from the people he had seen in the castle. This done, in complete silence they entered the room where he was asleep, resting from his recent scuffles. They moved up to where he lay tranquilly, not dreaming of any such thing, seized him firmly, and bound him fast hand and foot. When he woke up with a start he couldn't move, and could only marvel and wonder at the strange figures before him. He immediately gave way to the idea his crazed imagination always conjured up: he took it that all these shapes were phantoms of the enchanted castle, and that he himself was unquestionably enchanted, since he could neither move nor help himself — which was exactly what the curate, who had cooked up the scheme, expected. Of all those present, Sancho was the only one in his senses and his own proper character; and although he was within a hair's breadth of sharing his master's affliction, he did not fail to recognise who all these disguised figures were. But he didn't dare open his mouth until he saw what would come of this assault and capture of his master; and Don Quixote also said nothing, waiting to see how his predicament would end. The outcome was that they brought in the cage, shut him up in it, and nailed the bars so firmly they couldn't easily be broken open.

They then lifted him onto their shoulders, and as they were carrying him out of the room a terrifying voice — as terrifying as the barber (not the one of the pack-saddle but the other) could make it — was heard to say, "O Knight of the Rueful Countenance, let not this captivity in which thou art placed afflict thee; for thus must it be, for the speedier accomplishment of the adventure in which thy great heart hath engaged thee. The same shall be accomplished when the raging Manchegan lion and the white Tobosan dove shall be joined together, having first humbled their haughty necks to the gentle yoke of matrimony. And from this marvellous union there shall come forth into the light of the world brave whelps that shall rival the ravening claws of their valiant father; and this shall come to pass before the pursuer of the flying nymph hath, in his swift natural course, twice visited the starry signs. And thou, O most noble and obedient squire that ever bore sword at side, beard on face, or nose to smell with, be not dismayed or grieved to see the flower of knight-errantry carried off thus before thy very eyes; for soon, if it please the Framer of the universe, thou shalt see thyself raised to such a height that thou shalt not know thyself, and the promises thy good master hath made thee shall not prove false. And I assure thee, on the authority of the sage Mentironiana, that thy wages shall be paid thee, as thou shalt see in due season. Follow then in the footsteps of the valiant enchanted knight, for it is fitting that thou shouldst go to the destination assigned to you both; and as it is not permitted to me to say more, God be with thee, for I now return to that place I wot of." As he brought the prophecy to a close he raised his voice to a high pitch and then lowered it to such a soft tone that even those who knew it was all a joke were almost tempted to take what they heard seriously.

Don Quixote was greatly comforted by the prophecy, for he understood its meaning at once and perceived it was promising him that he would see himself united in holy and lawful matrimony with his beloved Dulcinea del Toboso, from whose blessed womb would come forth the whelps — his sons — to the eternal glory of La Mancha. Thoroughly and firmly persuaded of this, he raised his voice and with a deep sigh exclaimed, "O you, whoever you are, who have foretold so much good to me, I beg you, on my behalf, to entreat the sage enchanter who looks after my interests not to let me perish in this captivity in which they're now carrying me away before I see fulfilled such joyful and incomparable promises as those that have now been made to me. Let this only come to pass and I shall glory in the pains of my prison, find comfort in these chains they bind me with, and regard this bed they stretch me on, not as a hard battlefield, but as a soft and happy nuptial couch. And as for the consolation of Sancho Panza, my squire, I rely on his goodness and integrity not to desert me in good fortune or bad. If, by his ill luck or mine, it should not be in my power to give him the island I promised him, or some equivalent, at least his wages shall not be lost; for in my will, which is already drawn up, I have set down the sum to be paid him — measured not by his many faithful services but by the means at my disposal."

Sancho bowed his head very respectfully and kissed both his master's hands, for, being tied together, he could not kiss one. Then the apparitions hoisted the cage onto their shoulders and set it upon the ox-cart.
